title: Palm Royale
synopsis: Palm Beach, 1969. The most exclusive ball of the season has one empty seat and you intend to fill it. Smile. Lie beautifully.

nodes.text: The Palm Royale's brass doors have turned away a duchess, two Vanderbilts, and one woman whose only crime was a rented handbag. You have a borrowed Pucci, forty-one dollars, and a smile you rehearsed in three separate mirrors until it stopped looking like asking. The doorman raises exactly one eyebrow. He has all afternoon.

choices.text: Sweep past as if you own the place
choices.consequence: You walk in like a bill nobody wants to open. The doorman's hand comes halfway up and then, magnificently, changes its mind.

choices.text: Slip in through the cabana service path
choices.consequence: You go around the hedge in heels, which is a skill, and arrive at the pool from the direction the ice arrives from.

choices.text: Produce a forged sponsor's letter
choices.consequence: You hand over an envelope you steamed, typed, and aged with weak tea. Your hands do not shake. You practiced not shaking.

nodes.text: Evelyn Rollins arrives the way weather arrives. 'I don't know you,' she says, and in this zip code that is not an introduction, it is a diagnosis. Her gaze drops to your shoes and stays there long enough to price them, place them, and pity them. She holds a martini she has no intention of drinking.

choices.text: Drop a name she can't check
choices.consequence: You mention the Ashfords of Newport, who summer abroad and answer nothing. Evelyn's chin lowers a quarter inch. That is the entire victory.

choices.text: Compliment her late husband's foundation
choices.consequence: You praise the scholarship fund by its correct name. Evelyn softens exactly as much as a bank vault softens, which is enough.

nodes.text: Cabana row smells of coconut oil, chlorine, and inherited money, which has a smell of its own and the smell is cold. A pool boy named Robert folds towels and watches you not belong with genuine professional interest. One word from him and you become a story told at dinner. He doesn't say the word.

choices.text: Tip him your last bill for silence
choices.consequence: You press your last bill into a folded towel and hand it over. He takes it. Now you are broke and known, which is two problems.

choices.text: Ask him who really runs this place
choices.consequence: He laughs once without smiling. 'Not the ones with their names on the letterhead,' he says, and reaches for another towel.

nodes.text: The membership secretary reads your letter twice, holding it at the distance her eyes require and her pride denies. The signature is good. The letterhead is better — done in Miami by a man who prints wedding invitations and, occasionally, other things. 'Mrs. Donahue vouches for you,' she says. It isn't entirely a question.

choices.text: Insist, warmly, that you're old friends
choices.consequence: You describe a lunch in 1963 that never occurred, including what the soup was. The secretary writes your name in the book.

choices.text: Pivot to a different sponsor entirely
choices.consequence: You abandon Mrs. Donahue mid-sentence and produce a better name. Nimble — but the secretary has now watched you change horses.

nodes.text: At the bar you become a woman with a yacht in dry dock and a husband lost at sea, and Palm Beach leans in, because tragedy with money attached is the only conversation this room permits. It works beautifully for a solid twenty minutes. Then you notice the widow at the edge of it — Norma, in a wheelchair, who has not blinked once.

choices.text: Charm Norma directly
choices.consequence: You cross the room toward her, which nobody does. Norma watches you come the entire way and does not help you at all.

choices.text: Avoid her and work the younger set
choices.consequence: You turn to the girls with new money and newer teeth. They adore you instantly, which means nothing and costs nothing.

nodes.text: Evelyn, three drinks softer, mentions the card file. Norma keeps one: a name for every family in the county, and under each name the thing that family pays to keep quiet. Whoever holds the file holds the season, the ball, and the seating chart. It lives upstairs, in a room with a nurse in it.

choices.text: Plan to reach the file tonight
choices.consequence: You start counting staircases and nurses' shifts before Evelyn has finished her sentence. Ambition has appalling table manners.

choices.text: Decide the file is too dangerous to want
choices.consequence: You let it go, which is wise, and you will think about that card file at three in the morning for the next twenty years.

nodes.text: The bartender builds a grasshopper with the care of a man building something else entirely. 'They'll let you in,' he says, not looking up. 'They just never let anybody leave clean.' Then a key appears on the bar under two fingers — brass, stamped with a nine. Cabana 9. He goes back to the mint.

choices.text: Pocket the key
choices.consequence: The key is inside your glove before you have consciously decided anything. Your hand has always been faster than your conscience.

choices.text: Refuse it and stay visible
choices.consequence: You slide it back across the bar and stay where the light is. Whatever waits in Cabana 9 will find somebody else to ruin.

nodes.text: Somehow you are seated at the good table, between a Vanderbilt-adjacent and a woman who married three fortunes in the correct order. The conversation is entirely maiden names, deployed like map coordinates. Then someone sets down her fork, turns, and asks — pleasantly, fatally — where you summered as a girl. Eight women wait. Somebody's soup goes cold.

choices.text: Invent a lake nobody dares not to know
choices.consequence: 'Lake Tarrow, of course,' you say, and four women nod, because admitting ignorance would be worse than lying. Lake Tarrow does not exist.

choices.text: Turn the question back as a joke
choices.consequence: You ask where she summered and make it sound almost flirtatious. She talks for six minutes. You have purchased six minutes.

nodes.text: Robert finds you by the ferns. 'Norma's nurse takes her cigarette at four,' he says, to the middle distance, and walks off whistling something from a musical. He has decided you're interesting. In this town, being interesting to a man who sees everything and owns nothing is a particular kind of exposure.

choices.text: Time your move to four o'clock
choices.consequence: You check the clock above the bar twice and stop drinking. Whatever else you are tonight, you are a woman with a schedule.

choices.text: Win Norma over honestly instead
choices.consequence: You decide to go up at four and simply knock. It is the least strategic thought you have had since the bus left Ohio.

nodes.text: Models drift down a runway laid over the pool deck in next spring's clothes, and every woman watching does quiet arithmetic involving her waistline and her husband's accountant. Evelyn rests a hand on your arm. It could be affection. It could be a leash. A photographer circles the shallow end.

choices.text: Pose for the photographer
choices.consequence: You give him the profile you practiced. By Sunday your face is in the Shiny Sheet, captioned with a name that isn't yours.

choices.text: Slip out of frame
choices.consequence: You step behind a palm at precisely the right moment. Invisibility keeps you safe and keeps you nobody. That's the trade.

nodes.text: Dinah corners you by the lemonade with a smile like a paper cut. 'I had you looked into,' she says, delighted. 'And the funny thing, darling, is that you don't exist.' She hasn't told anyone yet. She is letting you watch her decide, and the watching is the part she enjoys. She takes a lemonade she doesn't want.

choices.text: Offer her something she wants
choices.consequence: You offer her the orchid committee chairmanship. She wants it so badly she forgets to ask how you'd possibly deliver it.

choices.text: Threaten her with a bluff
choices.consequence: You mention her husband's Tuesdays in Boca. You know nothing about his Tuesdays. Her face informs you that you do now.

nodes.text: Norma's hand closes on your wrist and it is iron, chair or no chair. 'You're a fraud,' she says, almost warmly. 'So was I. It's exhausting, isn't it — the arithmetic.' She looks you over the way a woman looks at a dress she might have altered, or a daughter she might invent.

choices.text: Confess everything to her
choices.consequence: You give her the town, the name, the debt, all of it, in under two minutes. Norma listens without a single flicker of surprise.

choices.text: Deny it and hold your shape
choices.consequence: You laugh it off with one hand on your pearls. Norma lets go of your wrist and looks disappointed in a way that stings for weeks.

nodes.text: Paddles rise for a diamond nobody in this room needs and everybody in this room requires. To bid is to be seen as somebody. To sit still is to be seen as nobody. The auctioneer is at four thousand and climbing. You have forty-one dollars, and one of them is folded inside a towel somewhere.

choices.text: Bid wildly on credit you don't have
choices.consequence: Your paddle goes up at nine thousand and the room turns to look at you with real respect. The invoice arrives Tuesday.

choices.text: Win the room without spending a cent
choices.consequence: You donate 'anonymously' in a stage whisper audible to three tables. It costs you nothing and buys you an entire season.

nodes.text: A card comes under the door sometime in the night. On it is your real name. Your real street. Your real mother, your real nothing at all. Under the banyan, midnight, it says, in handwriting deliberately slowed down to hide itself — or you get announced before the soup course.

choices.text: Go to the banyan tree
choices.consequence: You are standing under that tree at 11:52, because you have never once in your life been late to a threat.

choices.text: Burn the note and run the ball anyway
choices.consequence: You burn it in an ashtray shaped like a swan and go to bed. Sleep declines the invitation and does not send regrets.

nodes.text: Skeet Rollins, adrift on Demerol and four generations of citrus money, has taken a shine to you. He calls you by three different names in one conversation and finds all three delightful. His signature opens every account in the county. He is holding out a fountain pen and can't quite recall why.

choices.text: Take the pen and the access
choices.consequence: You take the pen. It's warm from his hand, and the name you sign with it is one you invented in a bus station.

choices.text: Decline, gently, and keep his trust
choices.consequence: You cap the pen and set it down on the tray. Skeet pats your arm and gets your name right, once, by accident.

nodes.text: Your story is fraying at the cuffs. A detail from Tuesday doesn't match a detail from Thursday, and two women behind two fans have compared them. Nobody says anything. Nobody here ever says anything. They simply stop refilling your glass and wait, because the season is patient and the season eats at eight.

choices.text: Get ahead of the rumor with a bigger one
choices.consequence: You feed the fans a story involving a senator and a houseboat. By Friday nobody can recall what they were checking on.

choices.text: Find an exit and an alibi
choices.consequence: You arrange to be seen in Boca on the night in question. Preparing to run is a kind of packing you've done before.

nodes.text: They're stringing the ballroom for tomorrow: ten thousand bulbs, orchids flown from somewhere expensive, and a man on a ladder arguing with a woman about the correct shade of gold. You will be standing in this room in twenty-six hours. Whether you stand in it as a guest or as a headline is still unsettled.

choices.text: Plan to be crowned the season's hostess
choices.consequence: You begin rewriting the seating chart in your head, and the ambition stops feeling like a plan and starts feeling like an appetite.

choices.text: Plan a quieter, safer triumph
choices.consequence: You aim lower on purpose: a good table, a kind word, no photographs. Restraint tastes like weak tea and keeps you breathing.

nodes.text: The press man has a photograph of you coming through the cabana door on day one, wrong shoes, wrong direction, wrong everything. He lets you hold it, which is the cruelty. 'Page six,' he says, 'or page nobody. Your choice — and then, someday, a favor.' He is extremely pleasant about it. They always are.

choices.text: Trade him a juicier secret
choices.consequence: You hand him Dinah's Tuesdays in Boca. He is thrilled. You have just discovered how easy that was, and it ought to trouble you more.

choices.text: Charm him into burying it
choices.consequence: You laugh at his joke and touch his sleeve and the negative goes into his pocket, unburned. He'll keep it. Of course he'll keep it.

nodes.text: The ballroom is on fire with light. Every name you have borrowed, bent, or broken is standing under one roof holding a drink. Evelyn taps a glass with her ring. At the dark edge of the room Norma sits alone, smiling at nobody in particular, which happens to be exactly how Norma smiles at you.

choices.text: Step into the light and take the floor
choices.consequence: You walk to the center of the room and the orchestra, reading the moment, changes songs for you. There is no going quiet after this.

choices.text: Work the margins and stay legible
choices.consequence: You stay near the columns, shaking hands two at a time, assembling a season out of small talk instead of spectacle.

nodes.text: Somebody presses a glass into your hand and four hundred faces rotate toward you at once. The orchestra has stopped. The waiters have stopped. Whatever leaves your mouth in the next fifteen seconds becomes, permanently, the truth about who you are in this town. You have a hundred lies ready and no plan at all.

choices.text: Toast to the season and your new life
choices.consequence: You raise the glass to the season and they raise theirs back, and the lie sets like concrete around both your feet.

choices.text: Toast to Norma — and tell the truth
choices.consequence: You say your actual name out loud into a silver room. Somewhere near the back, a woman in a wheelchair begins to laugh.

choices.text: Use the toast to expose the whole rotten club
choices.consequence: You name the ledgers, the affairs, and the charity fund that bought a boat. Four hundred people learn what real silence sounds like.

nodes.text: They are applauding. Not politely — properly, the way this room applauds a surname. You did it, in a borrowed dress, on forty-one dollars and nerve. Across the ballroom, by the doors, Robert gives you one small nod that is not congratulation. He is the only person here who remembers who walked in.

choices.text: Accept the crown and become Mrs. Palm Beach
choices.consequence: You accept the sash, the title, and the standing invitation. Ten seconds later a woman asks where you summered, and you answer without pausing.

choices.text: Walk out the front door, free and forty-one dollars richer
choices.consequence: You set the glass down mid-applause and start walking toward the brass doors. Nobody follows. Nobody here can imagine leaving.

nodes.text: You marry the correct surname and bury the incorrect one under thirty years of good linen. You chair the ball. You decide who sits where, and grown women rearrange their Decembers around your opinions. And every morning at six you wake with your heart going, certain that today is the day somebody remembers the cabana door. Nobody ever does. Not once in three decades — and that turns out to be the cruelest part of the arrangement.

Norma laughs until somebody has to thump her on the back, then instructs the staff to lay a permanent place at her table: third seat, view of the water. 'A fraud who admits it,' she wheezes, 'is only an ambitious woman with manners.' Evelyn never forgives you and never once excludes you, which in Palm Beach is a form of love. You keep the borrowed dress. You stop borrowing the name.

By Sunday the columns have all of it — the ledgers, the affairs, the orphans' fund that somehow bought a boat. The Palm Royale limps through two more seasons and then becomes a conference hotel with a widely praised buffet. You are not welcome anywhere south of Jupiter, which is fine, because you taught a ballroom full of queens that every crown in the building was rented. Including, in fairness, yours.

You leave the way nobody in that room has ever considered leaving: through the brass doors, upright, owing no one a maiden name. The valet asks which car. You tell him none. Behind you ten thousand bulbs burn for people who cannot get out of the building and know it. Ahead of you is a coast road, salt in the air, and forty-one dollars, which turns out to be precisely enough.
